Beethoven's Piano Sonata Number 23 in F minor, Opus 57, is widely known as the Appassionata. Composed in 1805, it's one of the most stormy and emotionally intense keyboard works of his middle period, created around the same time as his Eroica Symphony. The piece demonstrates his mastery of dramatic contrast and large-scale sonata form.

The nickname Appassionata, meaning passionate, wasn't actually given by Beethoven. A Hamburg publisher added it in 1838, decades after the work was composed. Beethoven dedicated the sonata to his friend and patron, Count Franz von Brunsvik, a Hungarian nobleman.

The first movement opens with a quiet, ominous unison theme in F minor that spans two octaves. This theme is repeated a half-step higher in G-flat major, then punctuated by explosive fortissimo outbursts. The second movement provides sharp contrast—a serene, chorale-like theme and variations in D-flat major. It ends with an unresolved, dissonant diminished seventh chord that flows directly into the finale. The third movement is a driving, restless perpetual motion finale back in F minor, marked by continuous sixteenth-note runs and dramatic sweep. It concludes with a frantic, dance-like coda at the fastest tempo.

Beethoven's early opera Fidelio, originally titled Lenore, shared this sonata's high-drama and tragic musical atmosphere. The Appassionata stands as a central masterpiece of Beethoven's middle heroic period, and the extreme dynamic shifts in the music mirror the intense light-and-shadow contrasts found in paintings by artists like Rembrandt.
